explanations.explanation: Thickets, friend. Isaiah says it plain: "In the thickets of Arabia you must lodge, O caravans of Dedanites." (Isaiah 21:13) The Dedanites are traveling people, and this is where they have to stay. I think a thicket makes a pretty scratchy hotel.

Cities would at least mean a roof and a door, but that's not what the text says. Isaiah says the caravans of Dedanites must lodge "In the thickets of Arabia" (Isaiah 21:13). Thickets are thick tangles of brush. I think that sounds a lot rougher than a city.

Arabia does sound like a desert kind of place, so I get why you picked it. But Isaiah says the Dedanites, a trading people who travel in caravans, must lodge "In the thickets of Arabia" (Isaiah 21:13). So picture brush, not open sand. Sometimes the text surprises us, and that's why we read it slow.

Water is the answer. Isaiah says, "Bring water for the thirsty, O dwellers of Tema" (Isaiah 21:14). Tema is a place in Arabia, and its people are the ones he's calling out to. A cold cup of water for someone in need is a simple thing to hand over.

Silver is shiny, but you can't drink it. Isaiah's words are "Bring water for the thirsty, O dwellers of Tema" (Isaiah 21:14). The thirsty need something for the thirst, and that's the water. Nobody ever got a dry throat fixed with a coin.

Tents are a decent guess, since these folks are on the move. But Isaiah says, "Bring water for the thirsty, O dwellers of Tema" (Isaiah 21:14). The word is water. A tent won't help a dry throat one bit.

True! Right after the water, Isaiah says, "meet the refugees with food" (Isaiah 21:14). So Tema is told to bring both drink and food. Refugees are people who have fled from their homes, and these ones show up needing a meal.

It's actually true. Isaiah tells the dwellers of Tema, "Bring water for the thirsty… meet the refugees with food" (Isaiah 21:14). So the text names food as well as water. Easy to skip right over that second part, so no worries.

explanations.answer: The sword and the bow in battle
explanations.explanation: That's it. Isaiah says they flee "from the sword—the sword that is drawn—from the bow that is bent, and from the stress of battle" (Isaiah 21:15). Swords and bows are the weapons right there in the verse. These folks ran from a fight, and that's why they need help.

explanations.answer: A great flood across the land
explanations.explanation: No flood in this one, friend. Isaiah says the refugees flee "from the sword—the sword that is drawn—from the bow that is bent, and from the stress of battle" (Isaiah 21:15). This is about war, with weapons ready. Keep your boots dry.

I'd run from locusts too, but they aren't in this verse. Isaiah says the refugees flee "from the sword—the sword that is drawn—from the bow that is bent, and from the stress of battle" (Isaiah 21:15). The danger here is battle, with swords and bows.

Yes, gone. The Lord says to Isaiah, "Within one year, as a hired worker would count it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone." (Isaiah 21:16) Kedar is a people of Arabia. A hired worker counts the time carefully, so it's a set year. All of it, not just some.

Doubled would be a nice surprise, but it's the opposite. The Lord says, "Within one year, as a hired worker would count it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone." (Isaiah 21:16) Kedar, a people of Arabia, loses it. Not a little of it, but all of it.

Dedan is in this passage, so I see why it caught your eye. But the Lord says, "Within one year, as a hired worker would count it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone." (Isaiah 21:16) The text says it will be gone, and it never says it passes to anyone. I'd stick to what the verse says.
Close, but it's the other way around. The Lord says, "The remaining archers, the warriors of Kedar, will be few." (Isaiah 21:17) Few, not many. Kedar's archers are shrinking down to just a handful.
False is right. The Lord says, "The remaining archers, the warriors of Kedar, will be few." (Isaiah 21:17) Few is the word. The archers of Kedar don't come out ahead here.
Israel it is. Isaiah closes with "For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken." (Isaiah 21:17) That's how the message ends, with the One who spoke it. Everything before it carries that weight.

Arabia fills the passage, so I see why you went there. But the verse ends, "For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken." (Isaiah 21:17) The word after "God of" is Israel. The message is about Arabia, but that's how Isaiah names the One who spoke.

Kedar is the last people named, so it's an easy slip. The verse ends, "For the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken." (Isaiah 21:17) Kedar is who the message was about, and Israel is the name that follows "God of." Plenty of bakers mix those up.
